title: Why Coding Agents Are Choosing Vercel as Often as Humans Do
summary: The rise of AI agents that write software continues to pay off for the companies that host such software. Among them is Vercel , whose software helps developers make and host websites and AI apps, including so-called agents that automate white-collar tasks. The 11-year-old company is generating $600 million in annualized revenue, or $50 million a month, up 148% from a year earlier and up from $500 million in July. The number of paying customers also rose by a similar amount, around 20%, according to a person close to the company. Valued at $9.3 billion in a financing a year ago, Vercel has since changed its business model and mostly charges customers based on their usage rather than through subscriptions. The company competes with an array of software firms, including Netlify and Cloudflare , as well as cloud providers like Amazon . And it’s also competing with OpenRouter , soon to be owned by Stripe , in helping app developers pick and choose the right AI models from one application programming interface. Coding AI agents that produce new code now account for about half of Vercel’s new business, up from less than 3% at the start of the year, CEO Guillermo Rauch said in June at Vercel’s Ship conference in London .

title: Microsoft’s Executive Exodus Foreshadows Business Transition
summary: Is there a fire alarm going off at Microsoft’s headquarters? A slew of Microsoft executives have bolted for the exits in recent weeks, most recently Ryan Roslansky, executive vice president of Office apps, who said Thursday he would leave at the end of this year. A day earlier it was Microsoft Science President Peter Lee ’s turn. Both follow a bunch of other senior exits over the past few months, most prominently Office and Windows chief Rajesh Jha. Those exiting are mostly veterans who had been at the company for 15 years or more. Each had their own reasons for leaving, we’d guess—for example, new jobs elsewhere. But it’s likely not a coincidence they’re choosing to leave as Microsoft, like other companies, is having to rethink how it operates to deal with both the opportunities and the threats posed by AI. In this environment, it makes sense that people who have been at Microsoft for years and probably have made a lot of money on the stock (it’s up 1,289% since 2014, according to Koyfin) would decide to get out now while the going is good.
